paras: The whipping death of a Mexican boy in Ramsey's Canyon took place about August 21, 1881, when a mob of about a dozen men in the Huachuca Mountains near Tombstone, Arizona Territory, forced Mexican woodcutters to flog a boy accused of insulting a girl. The boy was reported to have died of the beating, and the girl afterward said she had invented the story "for fun." The wire account ran in papers across the country, and the girl's father was arrested and examined before a magistrate at Charleston.

According to a Tombstone dispatch of August 31, the 13-year-old daughter of a man named Strand told her father that a Mexican boy had insulted her as she passed a Mexican wood camp in Ramsey's canyon. Later reports spelled the father's name Stroud.

The father raised a mob of a dozen men, went to the camp, took the boy, and made him take off his shirt. The men then compelled nine Mexicans, among them the boy's own father, to give him five blows each with a knotted rawhide thong; the father "begged off with two blows." Having done so, the mob left.

The fuller dispatch said the Mexicans set out for Sonora and that the boy died when they had gone about thirty miles and was buried near the line. The shorter wire version instead said the flogging resulted in his death "a few hours later."

Residents of Ramsey's canyon, fearing that the Mexicans would return to retaliate, drew up a petition asking the Sheriff for protection. No arrests had been made by August 31, but a dispatch of September 1 reported that Stroud had been arrested and was being examined before a magistrate at Charleston. A Tombstone correspondent wrote on September 3 that two local attorneys had spent two days at Charleston attending "the trial of the men ordering the whipping," and that while it was contended the boy died, the corpus delicti had not been proved. No report of the hearing's outcome or of an inquest appears in the coverage.

The short wire report, dated Tombstone or San Francisco, September 1, ran on September 2 and 3 from New York and Maine to Nevada, usually headed for the girl's falsehood: "Just for Fun," "Ghastly Fun.," "Did It For Fun." and "The Victim of a Girl's Lie." Other headlines centered the death, such as the New-York Tribune's "Flogged to Death" and the Alexandria Gazette's "Boy Flogged to Death," while the Portland Daily Press used "Beauties of Lynch Law" with the subhead "A Boy Unjustly Accused and Speedily Murdered." Some versions softened "a mob" to "a party of men" or "men," and a Lancaster rewrite garbled the story to say the Mexicans were driven from the camp and the boy "killed in the attack."

Western papers carried more detail and more comment. The Sacramento Record-Union headed the fuller dispatch "An Outrageous Crime—Boy Whipped to Death" and printed the follow-up under "The Whipping Outrage—Held for Murder." The Pioche Weekly Record called the participants "inhuman wretches," complained that none had been arrested, and wrote that it would have been "nothing more than justice" had the boy's father returned with friends and forced the girl's father to whip his own daughter. By the following week the story had become filler in Midwestern weeklies, where a ready-print "Tragical Tales" column said "the friends of the girl" made the Mexicans whip the boy until he died.

The reports differ on when the boy died: a few hours after the whipping in the wire version, or some thirty miles along the road to Sonora in the fuller Tombstone dispatch. The only local account written after the Charleston hearing began said the death had been contended but not proved.

bases: A mob of about a dozen men seized a Mexican boy at a wood camp over an alleged insult and forced other Mexicans to flog him, and he was reported to have died of it (A1, A2, A21).

A mob of about a dozen men, acting without authority to punish an alleged insult to a girl, had the boy flogged, and every dispatch reports he died of it (A1, A2, A21); the only local follow-up says his death had been contended but not proved at the Charleston hearing (A22), so the killing rests on report rather than a body or inquest.

Two separate Tombstone dispatches (A1, A2) and a Tombstone letter (A22) agree on the mob whipping, and the arrest of the girl's father is reported separately (A4, A14), though the boy's death was said not yet proved (A22).

framing.detail: The Sacramento Record-Union headed it 'An Outrageous Crime—Boy Whipped to Death' and called the mob's act a 'heilish purpose'.
The Portland Daily Press ran the wire under 'BEAUTIES OF LYNCH LAW / A Boy Unjustly Accused and Speedily Murdered.'
Most papers ran the short wire under headlines on the girl's lie, such as 'Just for Fun', 'Ghastly Fun.', 'The Result of a Lie.' and 'The Victim of a Girl's Lie.'
The Pioche Weekly Record called the mob 'inhuman wretches', faulted the lack of arrests, and said retaliation in kind would have been 'nothing more than justice'.
The Arizona Weekly Citizen's Tombstone letter treated the case as town gossip and noted the death was unproved.
